Volume 07 · Chapter 10

Three-statement forecasting

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c09

By the endBuild linked forecasts with a transparent financing policy.

Capability and prerequisites

You can turn operating assumptions into linked income, balance-sheet and cash-flow forecasts; specify how financing responds; and distinguish a balanced model from a feasible business plan. Use the statement identities, operating rollforwards, asset schedules, financing obligations, tax distinctions and ratio definitions. A spreadsheet is not necessary: a few equations, an explicit timeline and a checked opening balance sheet do the work.

A profitable distributor plans to grow. Its forecast shows earnings rising, yet its bank line is almost exhausted. Is growth unprofitable, are customers paying slowly, or has somebody entered capital expenditure twice? A linked forecast separates those mechanisms. It cannot establish that the customers will buy, the bank will lend, or the equipment will deliver its promised capacity.

1. Start with a decision and a driver map

A forecast is a statement about future outcomes under stated information and assumptions. A scenario is a specified combination of conditions, which need not have a probability attached. A budget can also assign targets and responsibility. Calling a desired sales target the “base case” does not supply evidence that it is likely. Preserve the distinction between observed opening balances, estimated relationships, contractual terms and managerial choices.

For a single product, quantity Q times unit price p gives revenue R = Qp. A quantity change and a price change interact: if quantities rise 10% and price rises 5%, revenue rises 1.10×1.05−1 = 15.5%, not 15%. For several products use ΣQjpj; changing product mix can alter gross margin even when every individual margin is unchanged. Recurring services may instead need customer counts, renewal rates, usage and recognized revenue per service period. State which events produce revenue and when cash is collected.

The MIT New Enterprises financial-plan assignment explicitly connects sales assumptions, operating costs, collection/payment timing and financing needs, and asks for sensitivities. That dated teaching brief motivates our workflow; none of its templates or example problems is reproduced here. Kothari's 2004 financial-analysis lecture likewise treats projected statements as expectations relevant to planning. An accounting identity is not an estimated demand equation.

A compact forecast input register
InputEvidence to seekConsequence to trace
Units and selling priceOrders, cancellations, market size, capacity and price responseRevenue, product costs, collections and required stock
Unit cost and cash overheadSupplier quotes, staffing and fixed/step commitmentsMargin and dated payments
Receivable/inventory/payable targetsAging, seasonality, lead times, credit terms and purchasesOperating cash tied up or released
Capital spending and useful livesAsset register, delivery dates, service capacity and maintenance needsInvestment cash, depreciation and productive capacity
Debt, tax and distributionsActual contracts, applicable rules and approved policiesInterest, tax, cash coverage and residual owner claims

An unsupported constant percentage should be an identified assumption, not disguised as an observed law. Damodaran's working-capital discussion explains why unusual historical changes and differing component behavior complicate forecasts. Here we model each component separately, exclude cash and interest-bearing debt from operating working capital, and keep the cash buffer and borrowing policy explicit. Supplier financing is not automatically permanent or free.

2. Build schedules before balancing cash

Use beginning and ending balances from the same entity, currency and period. With no writeoffs, returns, acquisition movements or currency effects, the receivable, inventory and payable identities give:

Customer receipts = revenue + opening receivables − closing receivables.
Purchases = cost of goods sold + closing inventory − opening inventory.
Supplier payments = purchases + opening payables − closing payables.

Thus COGS is neither purchases nor supplier cash unless the relevant stocks are unchanged. A payable target based on purchases uses a different denominator from one based on COGS. A days-based model must also specify the year length, average versus ending balance, credit-only versus total flows and the seasonal pattern. Twelve percent of annual sales as an ending receivable assumption is not evidence that every customer pays after exactly 43.2 days.

A capital schedule similarly starts with opening carrying amount, adds qualifying capital expenditure and subtracts depreciation and any explicitly modeled disposal or impairment. New expenditure can require cash before it produces revenue. Depreciation affects profit, but adding it back in the cash bridge does not reverse the investment payment. Forecast asset lives and service dates directly where material; mechanically setting depreciation equal to capex suppresses investment cycles.

Under a simple all-effects-in-profit case, ending equity is opening equity plus NI plus new contributions minus distributions. Current tax need not equal cash tax, and neither need equal total tax expense. Our main forecast deliberately stipulates identical book/tax depreciation, no temporary differences, positive taxable profits and full current payment, so one tax rate can be applied to positive PBT. These are fictional simplifications. An actual tax-loss year does not automatically generate an immediate refund.

3. Declare Lumen's entire forecasting contract

Lumen Instrument Supply is an original fictional distributor. Money is kCU, quantity is thousands of units and unit prices/costs are CU. Fifty thousand units at 10 CU generate 500 kCU. The two years are illustrative, not observations or forecasts for an actual firm. There are no acquisitions, foreign exchange, writeoffs, returns, deferred tax, leases, interest income, disposals or unlisted transactions. All sales and inventory purchases pass through receivables/payables; ordinary overhead is paid currently.

Opening balance sheet, kCU
AssetsAmountClaimsAmount
Cash20Trade payables25
Receivables40Term debt50
Inventory30Revolver0
Net operating equipment110Equity125
Total200Total200

Equity consists initially of capital 100 and retained earnings 25. The old equipment's remaining service pattern supports depreciation 20 in each modeled year. New equipment is bought at each year-end, begins service in the following year, and has a five-year straight-line life with zero residual. Year 1 capex of 50 therefore adds 10 to year 2 depreciation; year 2 capex of 30 has no depreciation within this horizon. No new shares are issued in the baseline.

Conditional operating and policy assumptions
DriverYear 1Year 2
Quantity / selling price / unit COGS50 / 10 / 6.560 / 10 / 6.5
Cash operating overhead100110
Closing AR / annual sales12%12%
Closing inventory / annual COGS20%20%
Closing AP / annual purchases10%10%
Cash capex / dividend50 / 1030 / 10

Term debt remains 50; none matures during the two-year horizon. Both debt types charge 10% on their opening balance, paid in the year. Revolver changes occur at the final date, coordinated with final-date capital spending and distributions, after the year's interest determination; new draws have no current-year interest under this exact teaching convention. Tax is 20% of nonnegative PBT and is paid in the same year. Tax and interest cash are operating, capex investing, and borrowing, debt repayment and dividends financing. These classifications are case choices, not claims about every current reporting framework.

The company targets minimum closing cash 20. Its separately stipulated available revolving line has maximum total outstanding balance 60. It draws only enough to reach the minimum or repays existing revolver with excess cash, without repaying the term loan. Once the revolver reaches zero, additional cash remains an asset. No undisclosed equity contribution or “other liability” can appear to force balance. Annual data do not establish feasibility at every day within the year; a monthly or finer cash calendar is a separate requirement for implementation.

4. First close operating performance, then financing

Worked example 1 — The linked two-year baseline

Year 1 revenue is 50×10 = 500; COGS is 50×6.5 = 325. Ending AR is 60 and inventory 65. Purchases are 325+65−30 = 360, so AP is 36. Receipts are 500+40−60 = 480; supplier cash is 360+25−36 = 349. Old-asset depreciation is 20. EBIT is 500−325−100−20 = 55. Interest on opening term debt is 5; tax is (55−5)×20% = 10 and NI is 40.

Direct CFO is 480−349−100−5−10 = 16. Operating working capital rises from 40+30−25 = 45 to 60+65−36 = 89, an increase of 44. Indirect CFO is also NI40 + depreciation20 − investment in working capital44 = 16. The company earns 40 but cannot spend all 40: most of its noncash earnings and depreciation addback are absorbed by customers and stock, partly financed by suppliers.

Cash before changing debt is 20+16−50−10 = −24. This is a financing requirement calculation, not a permissible negative cash asset. A draw of 44 restores closing cash to 20 and stays within the limit60. Net financing cash is 44−10 = 34. Ending equipment is 110+50−20 = 140; equity is 125+40−10 = 155. Assets285 equal AP36 + term debt50 + revolver44 + equity155.

Year 2 carries forward every closing stock. Revenue600 and COGS390 give AR72 and inventory78. Purchases are 390+78−65 = 403, so AP40.3. Customer receipts588 and supplier cash398.7 follow from the same rollforwards. Depreciation is 20+50/5 = 30. EBIT70 less interest(50+44)×10%=9.4 gives PBT60.6, tax12.12 and NI48.48.

The year 2 cash bridge is 48.48+30−20.7 = 57.78. Before revolver repayment, cash is 20+57.78−30−10 = 37.78; returning17.78 leaves the required20. It cannot repay all44 and preserve the buffer. The same events reconcile both yearly statements and the full horizon.

5. A financing rule is an equation with constraints

Let K be cash after operations, investment and the planned dividend but before the revolver adjustment; R0 is opening revolver and M minimum cash. With the main case's opening-debt interest convention, the desired change is ΔR = max(M−K, −R0). This caps repayment at the amount actually owed. Required closing debt is R1 = R0+ΔR. Accept the plan only if R1 is within the available limit and the other conditions are met. If K is large enough to repay everything, cash ends above M; it is not silently paid as an extra dividend.

Worked example 2 — Collections create a funding failure while earnings stay positive

Change only Lumen's year 1 AR target from12% to20% of sales. AR becomes100 instead of60; receipts fall40. With recognition, costs and tax unchanged, NI remains40. CFO falls from16 to−24, and K becomes20−24−50−10 = −64. Reaching cash20 requires a revolver84, exceeding the actual limit60 by24. Drawing the full60 would still leave a cash deficit4 and a shortfall24 against the required buffer. The unmodified plan is infeasible even though its income statement is profitable.

Canceling dividend10 reduces required borrowing to74, still14 beyond the limit. Delaying24 of capex instead reduces year 1 capex to26 and borrowing to60, reaching the buffer at equality under the maintained operating assumptions. Those assumptions matter: the deferred equipment must not be necessary for the sales and costs retained in the scenario. Its lower subsequent depreciation is not evidence that productive capacity is unaffected. New equity24 is another arithmetic repair if it can actually be raised on acceptable terms; neither lender capacity nor shareholder willingness follows from the model.

The program reports the shortage and stops before presenting a closing statement or later year as feasible. A line called “cash plug” that adds24 to assets without a funding event would erase the warning and break the economic story. A fabricated liability would balance the sheet but still not establish access to funds.

Scenario changes must propagate through all dependent schedules. Slower collections can increase next year's opening borrowing and interest; extra capex affects later depreciation; a dividend cut preserves equity as well as cash. Keep a change log showing which drivers changed and which were intentionally held fixed. Do not label a collection-only scenario a complete recession scenario: a recession might also affect quantities, prices, bad debts, inventory and refinancing terms.

6. Solve a genuine interest circularity

A different contract may charge interest on an average debt balance, so required borrowing increases interest, which in turn increases required borrowing. Repeated spreadsheet calculation can conceal this dependence. Derive the equation and check the branch before choosing a computational method.

For this separate one-period example, K now excludes revolver interest and its current tax relief as well as revolver financing, but includes every other cash event. The opening/closing mean debt is the explicitly stipulated interest base: I = r(R0+R1)/2. Tax rate τ applies with enough taxable profit to use all interest deductions currently. Let k = (1−τ)r/2. The cash identity is C = K − k(R0+R1) + R1−R0. On the positive-debt branch C=M, so

R1 = [M−K+(1+k)R0]/(1−k), provided 1−k > 0.

If this expression is negative, the policy instead closes debt at zero and retains excess cash; substituting zero in the cash identity checks that branch. A binding credit limit makes an otherwise positive solution infeasible. If tax relief cannot be used currently, replace that assumption and resolve the relevant tax branch. If actual interest uses dated daily balances, the beginning/ending mean is not an exact substitute unless justified by the contract or supplied timing.

Worked example 3 — Borrowing must finance its own interest

Supply K=−8, R0=10, M=20, r=10%, τ=20%, positive taxable profit before revolver interest30 and a line limit50. Then k=0.04 and R1=(20+8+1.04×10)/0.96 = 40. Interest is0.10×(10+40)/2 = 2.5; its current cash cost net of tax relief is2. Cash closes at−8−2+(40−10) = 20. Actual taxable profit27.5 remains positive, validating the assumed tax branch.

Ignoring that interest would give debt38. At38, actual interest2.4 costs1.92 after tax, leaving cash18.08. Conversely, charging interest on closing40 alone would impose4 instead of the stipulated2.5. The issue is the timing contract, not a choice of whichever formula balances most conveniently. If the limit were35, the shortfall at that limit would be4.8: −8−0.8×2.25+(35−10)=15.2. Five more debt would create4.8 of net usable cash because it also raises interest. A funding gap measured in cash need not equal the gap measured in gross debt.

7. Review the model and the decision separately

Check each opening balance, the direct and indirect CFO routes, debt and asset rollforwards, current/deferred tax treatment, equity movements, and A−L−E. Then inspect quantity/capacity, availability of credit, stock aging, collection assumptions and payout constraints. A formula can be internally consistent and factually unsupported. Conversely, an accounting error should be corrected before using the result as evidence of a weak business.

Stress one driver to understand a mechanism; combine related drivers to assess a coherent adverse scenario. For an uncertain input, report the assumption at which the decision changes, not just a percentage change in profit. Record whether cash is restricted and whether debt limits depend on a changing borrowing base or covenant. Lumen's fixed60 facility is deliberately simpler. Do not count the same supplier or lender capacity twice.

Make an implementation calendar from actual expected receipts and mandatory payments. Positive annual closing cash can conceal a midyear shortfall. Borrowing that only becomes available after a large payment cannot fund that payment. A monthly projection should itself reconcile to the annual statements, and particularly tight dates may need daily analysis. This chapter's annual checks are not a substitute for that calendar.

Download the original input contract, exact standard-library forecast and guide together. Run python3 v07-c10-analysis.py. It returns rational numbers, all three statements' components and explicit residuals. Modify a copy of the inputs, predict the propagation first, then compare. The code supplies no market observations, probabilities, bank approval or real tax rules.

Exercises

  1. Revenue drivers. Quantity rises from40 to44 thousand units and price from10 to10.5 CU. Find revenue in both periods and its percentage growth. Decompose the change into the old-price quantity effect, old-quantity price effect and interaction. Give two pieces of evidence needed before treating the new quantities and price as jointly attainable.
  2. Purchases are not COGS. Opening inventory30 and AP25 become inventory65 and AP36; COGS325. Find purchases and supplier cash. An analyst uses COGS minus the increase in AP as supplier cash. Quantify the error and explain which stock movement is missing.
  3. A collection improvement. Change only Lumen year1 closing AR to50 instead of60. Recompute receipts, CFO, revolver, equity and the closing balance sheet. Under the opening-debt interest rule, how much does this change year2 interest and NI if all other year2 operating and tax assumptions remain? Explain why the ten-unit first-year collection benefit cannot simply be added again next year.
  4. Repayment has a lower bound. In a separate opening-debt-interest case, K=80, opening revolver30, minimum cash20 and line limit60. Find repayment, closing debt and cash. Why is “set cash to20 and let debt be the balancing item” incorrect here? No extra payout or term-loan prepayment is authorized.
  5. Repair a funding failure. Use Lumen's20% year1 AR scenario. First cancel the10 dividend, then find the smallest additional capex deferral required to reach the cash20 target using a line no larger than60. Compute the repaired year1 closing assets, liabilities and equity. State the operational premise needed for this repair to preserve the supplied sales forecast.
  6. Solve another circularity. For the separate average-debt contract, use K=2, opening debt20, cash minimum25, rate10%, tax rate20% and limit50. Pretax profit before revolver interest is30. Derive required debt and interest, check the positive-tax-profit branch and reconcile cash. Then reduce the limit to40 and calculate the shortfall against minimum cash, using actual interest at that limit.
  7. Find a balanced but wrong model. An analyst subtracts Lumen's year1 capex50 as an extra income-statement expense while still adding it to PPE and reporting investing cash−50. The analyst still applies20% current cash tax to nonnegative PBT, and uses extra revolver borrowing to preserve cash20. Compute the wrong NI and compare CFO obtained directly from receipts/payments with CFO obtained indirectly from that NI. For each CFO route, compute required borrowing, closing equity and A−L−E; identify the contradiction even when the balance sheet balances. Explain why inserting an additional50 of equity does not repair the model. Assume the fictional tax law permits only the supplied depreciation, not immediate expensing of that equipment.
  8. Annual success, dated failure. A separate plan has opening cash5. A mandatory payment30 occurs on31March; the only customer receipt40 arrives30September; no other cash flows occur. The target is merely nonnegative cash. Compute year-end cash and the required temporary financing before the receipt. If a proposed loan becomes available only1April, is the plan feasible at the payment date? Give a specific possible repair and identify the assumption it changes.
Complete solutions
  1. Revenue moves from400 to462, a62 increase or15.5%. The components are(44−40)×10=40,40×(10.5−10)=20 and(44−40)(10.5−10)=2, totaling62. Evidence could include demand at the higher price, cancellations/competitive alternatives, production capacity, customer credit and delivery commitments. Name at least two and explain which assumed driver each tests; merely observing past growth does not establish simultaneous price and quantity increases.
  2. Purchases=325+65−30=360. Supplier cash=360+25−36=349. The mistaken325−11=314 understates cash outflow by35, exactly the inventory buildup. Cost of sold units excludes the newly purchased unsold inventory, which still needs financing.
  3. Receipts rise from480 to490; CFO rises from16 to26; K becomes−14 and the draw34. NI40 and equity155 are unchanged. Assets cash20+AR50+inventory65+PPE140=275; claims AP36+term50+revolver34+equity155=275. Year2 interest falls by10%×10=1, raising NI by0.8 at the20% tax rate. But opening AR is ten lower; with year2 closing AR still72, its increase is22 rather than12. The earlier collection cannot be collected again. Its financing-cost benefit differs from a permanent extra customer receipt.
  4. The company can repay only30, leaving debtzero and cash50. Algebraically ΔR=max(20−80,−30)=−30. Forcing cash20 by a repayment60 would create debt−30, an invented lender asset or unapproved additional use of cash. Preserve cash50 unless another authorized transaction is separately modeled.
  5. Original required debt is84. Canceling dividend10 reduces it to74; deferring another14 of capex reduces capex from50 to36 and debt to60. CFO remains−24;20−24−36+60=20. PPE=110+36−20=126. Assets20+AR100+inventory65+PPE126=311. AP36+term50+revolver60=146, and equity125+NI40−dividend0=165; total311. The deferred investment must not undermine the forecast operating capacity, quality, costs or legal commitments; otherwise revise those drivers and resolve. The arithmetic does not establish that premise.
  6. k=0.04. Required debt=(25−2+1.04×20)/0.96=365/8=45.625. Interest=0.10×(20+45.625)/2=3.28125. PBT=26.71875>0 validates full current tax relief. After-tax interest2.625 gives cash2−2.625+(45.625−20)=25. With the lower limit40, interest is3 and cash2−2.4+(40−20)=19.6, a5.4 shortfall. Gross required debt exceeds40 by5.625; after financing its own interest, the extra cash effect is0.96×5.625=5.4.
  7. The wrong EBIT is55−50=5; after interest5, wrong PBT, tax and NI arezero. The wrong cash tax is ten below the supplied law. Direct CFO would then be480−349−100−5=26, while the analyst's indirect route NI0+depreciation20−ΔNWC44 gives−24. The routes already disagree by50. If the analyst uses that wrong indirect CFO, K=20−24−50−10=−64 and borrowing84 is needed, also breaching the limit. Assets remain285; claims are AP36+term50+revolver84+equity(125+0−10=115)=285: this internally balanced sheet conceals the contradictory direct cash and tax treatment. If the analyst instead uses direct CFO26 and borrowing34, claims sum235 andA−L−E=50. The two requested routes expose different manifestations of the same erroneous recognition. Neither variant is correct. Inserting50 into equity supplies neither a real owner cash contribution nor the correct profit/tax entries. Restore NI40, tax10, CFO16, draw44 and equity155; record capex only as the asset/cash transaction plus its specified future depreciation.
  8. Year-end cash would be5−30+40=15, but the31March deficit is25. Financing must be available by that date; a1April loan is too late. A committed draw available by31March of at least25, a legally agreed payment deferral until after funding, or an earlier customer advance could repair the timing. State which lender/contract/customer timing assumption changes and verify it; an annual positive closing balance alone does not do so.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain why Lumen earns40 in year1 yet needs44 of new borrowing while its cash stays20. Name the operating, investing and owner-distribution effects and explain why the available line is a constraint rather than an accounting identity.

Teach-back benchmark

NI40 plus noncash depreciation20 gives60 before working-capital investment44; CFO is16. Starting cash20 plus16 cannot cover capex50, dividend10 and the required ending20 without borrowing44. Operating balances, asset spending and distributions are different uses of resources. The stipulated limit60 admits the baseline but excludes required debt84 under slow collections. A balanced forecast cannot persuade the bank to lend beyond its actual commitment.

Delayed check, one week later. Keep baseline year1 except capex is40 instead of50. Predict year1 CFO, NI, revolver, equipment and equity; then state the effects on year2 depreciation, interest and NI before calculating the rest of year2. Assume the operating plan remains feasible despite the smaller investment.

Delayed-check answer

Year1 CFO16 and NI40 are unchanged because new assets begin service next year. Revolver becomes34, equipment130 and equity155; closing cash remains20. Year2 depreciation falls from30 to28 and opening-debt interest from9.4 to8.4. EBIT rises2 and interest falls1, so NI rises3×0.8=2.4, from48.48 to50.88. That lower reported cost does not demonstrate that forgone equipment is economically harmless. Verify the capacity/maintenance premise before recommending the reduction.

Continue to accounting standards, disclosure and comparability. A model needs compatible definitions and versions as well as linked formulas. All models, numerical contracts and problems here are original; linked dated teaching sources support the stated methods, not an actual financing or tax recommendation.

Sources and further study

  • MIT OpenCourseWare 15.390 New Enterprises (Spring 2013), Assignment 9 — Financial Section — Dated teaching support for explicit sales/cost assumptions, sensitivity, linked earnings/cash projections, working-capital timing and identification of financing amounts, dates and terms. Original chapter case and exercises do not reproduce the source assignment or its template.
  • S. P. Kothari, MIT 15.511 Corporate Accounting (18 June 2004), Financial Statement Analysis — Historical lecture orientation to operations/investment/financing analysis and pro forma statements as expectations for evaluation and planning; does not supply the author's financial forecast formulas or numerical contracts.
  • Aswath Damodaran, Working capital in valuation (undated faculty-hosted method page) — Operating working-capital perimeter, unstable historical changes, relation to sales/COGS and distinct component behavior; caution about assuming indefinite releases or costless supplier financing. Lumen's separate purchase-based AP driver is an author-supplied convention.
